How to Build an Approval…


On this page (20)


An approval workflow moves each request from the person who asks, to the person who checks, to the person who signs off. It also chases anyone who sits on a request. This guide shows how to build one without code in[Taskade Genesis](https://www.taskade.com/ai/apps) , five other ways to do it, and when each one is the better fit. To compare automation tools side by side, read our list of the[best AI automation tools](https://www.taskade.com/blog/best-ai-automation-tools) .


## Quick answer


To build an approval workflow without code, you need five things: a request form, a list of who approves at each stage, a rule that moves each request to the next approver, a log of every decision, and a daily check that escalates overdue items. Jotform has a free plan with 5 forms and 100 submissions a month. Taskade Genesis builds all five parts in one app, and you change the approval limits in a table instead of in code.


The rest of this page covers what each part does, the three steps to build it, the four kinds of approval, templates by request type, a worked example, what it costs, five other ways to do it, and the limits to know before you start.


## What a working approval workflow needs


A working approval workflow needs five parts, and a missing part is the reason most approvals end up in a long email thread. A form that asks for the same facts every time stops the "what is this for?" reply. An approver map stops the "who signs this?" question. A hand-off, a log and an overdue alarm stop the chasing.


Part What it looks like How Taskade does it


Request form "Supplier payment, $4,200, due 30 Nov" A form in the app adds a row to the Requests project


Approver map Up to $500 the manager, up to $10,000 finance, above that the CEO One project: stage, amount limit, approver email


Hand-off The manager approves, finance gets it next A Field Updated trigger, then Assign Task and an email


Decision log Who approved what, and when Each status change adds a row to an Audit log project


Overdue alarm 2 days with no decision, the next level gets it A weekday Schedule trigger, Find Task(s), reassign, email


All five parts run on built-in Taskade automation steps: the form trigger,[Field Updated](https://www.taskade.com/learn/automation/field-updated) ,[Assign Task](https://www.taskade.com/learn/automation/assign-task) ,[Branch](https://www.taskade.com/learn/automation/branch-action) ,[Find Task(s)](https://www.taskade.com/learn/automation/find-tasks) , email notifications and the[Schedule](https://www.taskade.com/learn/automation/schedule) trigger. No connector is needed, and none of these steps use AI credits.


The flow below shows one request from the form to payment. The overdue check is a separate forward branch, so a late request jumps to the next level instead of waiting.


### The approver map is the part people skip


The approver map is one small table, and it decides who sees each request. Write it before you build anything. A typical map for a 10 to 50 person business has three rows.


Stage Amount limit Approver Backup when away


1. Manager Up to $500 The requester's manager Another manager


2. Finance Up to $10,000 Finance lead The CEO


3. CEO Above $10,000 CEO Finance lead (record the reason)


Keep the limits in this table, not in the automation. When a limit changes, you edit one cell and the router reads the new number on the next request. The free[approval matrix template](https://www.taskade.com/templates/operations-intelligence/approval-matrix) gives you a ready table to start from.


### Real approval apps that customers run


Two anonymised patterns from teams that run approvals on Taskade Genesis show the two common shapes:


- A construction group's finance team in Vietnam sends every supplier payment through 3 approvals in one Taskade Genesis app: accounting proposes, internal control reviews, and the CEO signs off.
- An internal team runs a multi-stage approval tracker on Taskade Genesis: new requests go to the right approver, every status change lands in an audit log, and a daily check escalates overdue items. The log holds about 270 entries.


The first is a fixed chain, where every request passes every stage. The second routes each request to one approver and escalates on time. The build below supports both: set the Branch step to "every stage" or "one stage by amount".


## Which kind of approval do you need?


Most small-business approvals are one of four kinds: serial, parallel, conditional or auto-approved below a limit. Serial means one approver after another. Parallel means two approvers decide at the same time. Conditional means the amount or the department picks the path. Pick the kind before you build, because it decides how many decision fields and automation paths the app needs.


Kind How it works Example How to build it in Taskade


Serial Each approver signs after the one before Supplier payment: manager, then finance, then CEO A Field Updated trigger on Status assigns the next approver


Parallel Two approvers review at the same time A contract: legal and finance Give each approver a decision field. A Branch step sets Approved only when both fields say Approved


Conditional A value on the request picks the path Above $10,000 goes to the CEO A Branch step reads the amount or the department


Auto-approve Small requests skip review but still get logged Office supplies under $100 One Branch path sets Status to Approved, and the Logger still writes a row


A Branch step holds up to 7 paths, and each path can require several conditions that must all be true. That is what makes the parallel kind work: the path that moves a contract forward checks both decision fields. The[Branch guide](https://www.taskade.com/learn/automation/branch-action) shows how to add a Fallback path, so a request that matches no rule still lands with a person.


Mix the kinds freely. A common small-business setup auto-approves under $100, sends $100 to $500 to the manager, and sends anything with a contract attached to legal and finance in parallel.

## Build it in Taskade in 3 steps


You build the approval app in three steps: create the app, fill the approver map and sign-ins, then switch on three automations. Test it with one small request and one large request before your team uses it. The first build takes an afternoon for most teams, and most of that time goes into the approver map.


For the click-by-click version, follow the[approval workflow tutorial](https://www.taskade.com/learn/genesis/approval-workflow) in Learn Taskade.


### Step 1: Create the approval workflow app


[Build the approval workflow app with Taskade EVE](https://www.taskade.com/create?prompt=Build%20an%20approval%20workflow%20app.%20Staff%20submit%20a%20request%20with%20amount%2C%20reason%20and%20due%20date.%20Requests%20up%20to%20%24500%20go%20to%20the%20manager%2C%20up%20to%20%2410%2C000%20to%20finance%2C%20and%20above%20that%20to%20the%20CEO.%20Log%20every%20status%20change%20in%20an%20audit%20log.%20Every%20weekday%20morning%2C%20find%20requests%20with%20no%20decision%20for%202%20days%2C%20assign%20them%20to%20the%20next%20approver%20and%20email%20them.&utm_source=landing_blog&utm_medium=howto&utm_campaign=build-approval-workflow&entry_kind=content&source=blog&entry=%2Fblog%2Fbuild-approval-workflow) . The link opens[Create](https://www.taskade.com/create?entry_kind=content&source=blog&entry=%2Fblog%2Fbuild-approval-workflow) with this prompt filled in:


> Build an approval workflow app. Staff submit a request with amount, reason and due date. Requests up to $500 go to the manager, up to $10,000 to finance, and above that to the CEO. Log every status change in an audit log. Every weekday morning, find requests with no decision for 2 days, assign them to the next approver and email them.


Taskade EVE builds the request form, three projects (Requests, Approvers and Audit log) and the app screens. Edit the prompt first if your stages or limits differ. A build from a prompt uses[AI credits](https://www.taskade.com/learn/genesis/model-credits) . On Free, you earn free AI credits with referrals and invites, and you can upgrade any time. Pro includes 50,000 AI credits a month. If you want to start by hand, copy the[approval matrix template](https://www.taskade.com/templates/operations-intelligence/approval-matrix) into a project and add the form yourself. The[first app guide](https://www.taskade.com/learn/genesis/first-app) walks through the editor.


A good request form asks for the same six facts every time:


Field Type Why it matters


What is it for Short text The approver reads it first


Amount Number The router reads it to pick the stage


Supplier or payee Short text Finance needs it to pay


Due date Date The overdue check counts from it


Attachment File A quote or an invoice stops the "send me the PDF" email


Requested by Email The decision email goes back to this person


To show or hide questions by answer (for example, ask for a purchase order number only above $1,000), add conditional logic to the form in the editor.


### Step 2: Map your approvers and their sign-ins


Open the Approvers project and add one row per stage: the stage name, the amount limit and the approver's email. Add a Status field to the Requests project with these values: Submitted, Manager review, Finance review, CEO review, Approved, Rejected and Paid.


Then publish the app and invite each approver. App sign-in works on every plan, Free included, and[App Users](https://www.taskade.com/learn/genesis/app-users) explains the set-up. Sign-in confirms who the approver is. To show each approver only the requests assigned to them, match each request to the approver's email, and test it with a second account. Inside the workspace, role-based access runs from Owner to Viewer, so a requester can read a request without the right to approve it.


The statuses form one forward path. A rejected request ends, and the requester submits a new one with the fix. That keeps the log simple to read.


### Step 3: Turn on routing, the decision log and the overdue check


Open **Automations** and switch on three automations. Each one is short, and each one does one job.


Automation Starts when What it does


1. Router A new request is added Branch reads the amount, Assign Task picks the first approver, an email tells them


2. Logger The Status field changes Adds a row to the Audit log: who, from, to, when


3. Overdue check Every weekday at 08:00 Find Task(s) lists requests waiting 2+ days, assigns the next level, emails them


The Router reacts to new rows. The Logger reacts to the[Field Updated](https://www.taskade.com/learn/automation/field-updated) trigger, so it also writes the moment a request is approved or rejected. The Overdue check uses the[Schedule](https://www.taskade.com/learn/automation/schedule) trigger with a time zone, so 08:00 means 08:00 where your team works. To act on a fixed due date instead of a waiting time, use the Task Due trigger.


The sequence below shows a $5,000 request where the finance lead is away for two days.


Test the app with two requests before your team uses it:


1. Submit a $200 request. Check that it goes to the manager only, and that the Audit log gets one row when you approve it.
2. Submit a $5,000 request and leave it. On the next weekday after 2 days, check that the overdue check assigned it to the next level and sent the email.


When both pass, share the form link with your team and retire the email thread.

A 25-person company with 60 requests a month uses about 290 automation runs, so it fits Pro with room to spare. Each automation counts one run from trigger to finish. ## Five mistakes that slow approvals down


Five mistakes cause most slow approvals in a new app: too many rules on day one, a requester who cannot see the stage, no escalation, limits hidden inside the automation, and a log that nobody reads. Each one has a short fix.


1. **Build every exception on day one.** Start with the three-row approver map. Add a rule only after a real request needs it.
2. **Keep the requester in the dark.** Show the Status on the request and send the decision email. That stops the "where is my request?" message.
3. **Skip the escalation.** Without the overdue check, one person on leave stops every request at their stage.
4. **Put the limits inside the automation.** Keep amounts in the Approvers table, so a finance lead can change $10,000 to $15,000 without opening the automation.
5. **Never read the log.** Look at the Audit log once a month. Find the requests that waited longest and the stage that held them.

## Limitations: when Taskade is not the right fit


Choose a dedicated tool if an approval must carry a legal e-signature, post the payment to your accounting system, or pass an external audit. Taskade keeps a clear decision log, but the log is not a signed, tamper-proof record.


- **You need a legal e-signature on each approval.** Taskade has no DocuSign connector. Approvers approve in the app.
- **The approval must post to QuickBooks or Xero.** Taskade has no QuickBooks or Xero connector. A webhook to your own system is Pro and up.
- **An external auditor must trust the log.** A workspace owner can edit the Audit log project. Use a system with a locked audit trail.
- **You run 50+ step processes across departments.** A process platform such as Kissflow is built for that scale.
- **You want approvers to decide by replying to an email.** Approvers open the app to set the status.


## FAQ


Can I build an approval workflow without code?


Yes. An approval workflow needs five parts: a request form, a list of approvers by stage and amount, a rule that hands each request to the next approver, a log of every decision, and a daily check for overdue items. In Taskade Genesis you describe those parts in plain English and get one app with the form, the tables and the automations.


How does a request move to the next approver?


An automation watches the Status field. When the manager sets a request to Approved, the automation assigns the request to the next approver on the list and emails them. Nobody forwards anything by hand, and the requester can see the current stage in the app.


Can I route approvals by amount?


Yes. A Branch step in the automation reads the amount on the request and picks a path. A common setup sends requests up to $500 to the manager, up to $10,000 to finance, and anything larger to the CEO. You change the limits in one approver table, not in the automation.


What happens when an approver is away or late?


A scheduled check runs every weekday morning. It finds requests that waited 2 days or more with no decision, assigns them to the next level, and emails that person. You pick the number of days and the time of day.


Does the app keep a history of every decision?


Yes. A second automation adds a row to an Audit log project each time a status changes: who changed it, from what, to what, and when. The log is a clear record for your team. It is not a signed, tamper-proof record for an external audit, because a workspace owner can edit it.


Can approvers sign in to the app?


Yes. App sign-in works on every plan, Free included. Sign-in confirms who the approver is. To show each approver only the requests assigned to them, match each request to the approver's email, and test it with a second account before your team uses it.


How much does it cost to run approvals in Taskade?


Free has 3 apps, 2 members and 10 automation runs a month, and it starts with no AI credits. A daily overdue check uses a run every weekday, so a live approval app needs Pro at $10 a month billed annually ($20 monthly), with 1,000 runs and up to 10 members. Pro also connects up to 10 custom domains, and Business at $25 a month billed annually connects unlimited custom domains.


What is the difference between serial and parallel approval?


In a serial approval, each approver signs after the one before, for example manager, then finance, then CEO. In a parallel approval, two approvers review at the same time, for example legal and finance on a contract. In Taskade you build a parallel approval with one decision field for each approver and a Branch step that moves the request on only when both say Approved.


Can approvers approve from a phone?


Yes. A published Taskade Genesis app is a web link, so an approver opens it in a phone browser, reads the request and sets the status. The decision email also links back to the request. Approvers cannot approve by replying to the email.


When is Jotform, Power Automate or Kissflow the better choice?


Jotform fits when the form is the main job and you want a drag-and-drop approval flow. Power Automate fits a company that already runs on Microsoft 365. Kissflow fits large processes across many departments with a sales-led contract. Pick Taskade Genesis when approvals sit next to the rest of your team's work in one app.
